newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE in first fund, allows some foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: UAE in first fund, allows some foreign investment.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates is opening an investment window to international cash by allowing foreigners to own units in the country's first equity fund, the fund's managers said on Monday.

"The Emirates Equity Fund is the first ever mutual fund that offers the public a chance to participate in the booming UAE equities market," said Anis al-Jallaf, chief executive of Emirates Bank International (EBI).

"For the first time non-UAE nationals will be allowed to participate in this fund, up to a maximum 20 percent...We have (central bank) approval for only 20 percent. It is a first step, we might change it later," he told a news briefing.
In the past year the market, capitalised at around 64 billion dirhams ($17.4 billion), has moved up about 30 percent.
About three-quarters of the UAE's 2.4 million people are foreigners, who have so far been excluded from the market.
Jallaf said the EBI fund would be a "test" for any future funds on the market, which is currently informal.
For years, the UAE has been working at setting up an official exchange and analysts hope the March appointment of a new economics minister might speed up the process.
Like its Gulf Arab neighbours, the UAE is trying to give the private sector a bigger role in its state-dominated economy and cut reliance on the 2.2 million barrels of oil it pumps daily.
It is also trying to widen investment opportunities at home and repatriate funds, estimated by analysts to run into tens of billions of dollars, invested in the West's developed markets.
Most Gulf Arab states say they are eager for foreign investment in their oil economies but have yet to fully open their bourses to international cash.
Jallaf said the new mutual fund would invest in the most active of the 30-odd companies traded regularly on the market.
The minimum investment is 10,000 dirhams and subscription will be open for a month from June 1.
"It is open-ended. We have chosen 22 stocks so far, but that is variable. We will be starting with (investment of) about 30 million dirhams," said EBI treasury manager Suresh Kumar.
He expected the fund to add liquidity to the market, where trade accounts for only five percent of market capitalisation.

This compares to Cairo where turnover is around 19 percent of market capitalisation of some $18 billion. In nearby Kuwait average trade value was $19.3 billion last year against average market capitalisation of around $18 billion.
Warning that there might be some controversy over the move to permit foreign participation, Jallaf made clear that unit holders would not be given any rights in individual stocks.
"It will not give any non-UAE nationals any rights in the shares, but just give them the chance to benefit from overall share appreciation. That is why it was allowed," he said.
EBI is 80 percent owned by the government of UAE member Dubai. The rest is held by about 750 private investors.
